blocks.prompt: The Rose That Never Had Thorns
blocks.text: People say a rose has thorns. That is not quite right. A rose has prickles. A thorn grows from deep inside a branch, so it is stuck there for good. A prickle grows on the skin of the stem, a bit like a fingernail. You can snap a prickle off with your thumb. The rose uses its prickles like tiny hooks. They grab onto other plants, and the rose pulls itself up toward the sun. After the petals fall off, a small red fruit grows where the flower used to be. It is called a rose hip. Birds eat the hips all winter long.

blocks.prompt: The Rose Is an Apple's Cousin
blocks.text: Look closely at an apple blossom in spring. Five pale petals, a ring of yellow stamens in the middle, and a sweet smell. Now look at a wild rose. Five pink petals, a ring of yellow stamens in the middle, and a sweet smell. They look almost the same because they are family. Roses belong to a group of plants called the rose family. So do apples, pears, plums, cherries, peaches, strawberries, raspberries, and almonds. If you have eaten a strawberry, you have eaten a cousin of the rose. The big roses in a flower shop look nothing like that. They have dozens of petals packed in tight. Almost every wild rose has only five. The extra petals came from us. Long ago, gardeners spotted roses whose stamens had turned into petals by mistake, and they kept planting those ones on purpose. Hundreds of years later, we have roses stuffed with petals. Roses make fruit too. Once the petals drop, the base of the flower swells into a red rose hip with the seeds tucked inside. It really is a fruit, and it really is a relative of the apple in your lunch.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit Nobody Wanted Until They Needed It
blocks.text: In 1941, Britain ran out of oranges. The war had closed the shipping lanes, and the ships that once carried fruit were carrying other things now. Oranges simply stopped arriving. That was more serious than a lost treat. Bodies need vitamin C to build collagen, the material that holds skin and blood vessels together. Without enough of it over months, people develop scurvy: bleeding gums, wounds that will not close, old injuries reopening. The answer had been growing in the hedgerows the whole time, free, and nobody had bothered with it. When a wild rose finishes flowering, the base of the flower swells and hardens into a red fruit called a rose hip. Weight for weight, a rose hip carries far more vitamin C than an orange does. It had been sitting on roadsides and field edges for centuries, feeding birds and no one else. So the government asked the children. Schools sent classes out along the lanes with baskets and gloves, and paid them a few pence for every pound of hips they carried back. Hundreds of tons came in. Factories boiled the hips, strained out the seeds and the fine itchy hairs packed around them, and bottled the result as rose hip syrup. Clinics handed it out by the spoonful to babies and small children, all through the winter. The odd part is that nothing changed about the rose. It was exactly as useful in 1938 as it was in 1941. What changed was that the oranges stopped coming, and people finally looked at the hedge.

blocks.prompt: Picked Before the Sun Gets Warm
blocks.text: In the Valley of Roses, in central Bulgaria, the working day starts in the dark. Pickers reach the fields by five in the morning and move down the rows by feel as much as by sight, snapping damask roses off just below the flower and dropping them into sacks tied at the waist. By ten they stop. Not because they are tired, but because the roses have stopped being worth picking. Rose scent is not a smell in the way we usually imagine it. It is a set of small, light molecules sitting in the petal, drifting off into the air, which is the only reason your nose ever finds them. Warmth makes them drift faster. A rose left in the sun for three hours has quietly released a good share of the thing that makes it valuable. Pick it at five and the oil is still in the flower. Pick it at noon and much of it is somewhere over the next field. What happens next is hard to picture honestly. The petals go straight to a still, where steam pulls the oil out of them, and the product is attar of roses, a pale liquid that smells overwhelmingly, almost unbelievably, of rose. It takes roughly three thousand kilograms of petals to make one kilogram of attar. That is a truckload of flowers for a bottle you could close your hand around. Attar sells by the gram, and it is one of the most expensive agricultural products in the world. Meanwhile, in a supermarket, you can buy a dozen long stemmed red roses that smell of almost nothing at all. That is not laziness and it is not an accident. Those roses were built to solve a different problem. A florist rose has to hold a straight stem, survive a refrigerated flight from Ecuador or Kenya, resist disease in the greenhouse, open slowly in a vase, and arrive with its color intact. Every one of those traits was chosen for, season after season, by people deciding which plants got to have offspring. Scent was not on the list. A plant has only so much energy to spend, and what the breeders stopped asking for, the rose quietly stopped making. A flower is an advertisement aimed at insects. We rebuilt this one into a machine for surviving a supply chain, and then we acted surprised when the advertisement went quiet.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Genus Rosa, family Rosaceae
Roses cannot make delphinidin, the blue pigment
Applause, the engineered blue rose, came out mauve
Yellow roses trace to Rosa foetida, around 1900
One enzyme, RhNUDX1, makes the rose scent geraniol
About 150 wild species, tens of thousands of garden kinds

blocks.prompt: The Color the Rose Cannot Make
blocks.text: There is no blue rose. There never has been. Florists sell them dyed or airbrushed, and catalogs list varieties with names like Blue Moon that turn out, when they open, to be a disappointed shade of lilac. The reason is not that nobody has tried hard enough. The reason is written into the plant. Flower color in roses comes mostly from a group of pigments called anthocyanins. Which anthocyanin a plant builds depends on which enzymes it has, and which enzymes it has depends on which genes it carries. Cyanidin gives magenta and red. Pelargonidin gives orange and scarlet. Delphinidin gives blue and violet, and it is the pigment behind delphiniums, pansies, and violets. The rose does not carry a working copy of the gene for the enzyme that makes delphinidin. This is not a matter of degree or effort. The rose cannot take that step, and no amount of crossing one rose with another rose will conjure a gene that no rose has. In 2004, a Japanese company announced the only thing that could work. Researchers had inserted a delphinidin gene borrowed from a pansy, along with a gene from an iris, into a rose. The plant made delphinidin. The flower, sold as Applause, is mauve. Rose petals are mildly acidic, and delphinidin shows a different color depending on the acidity around it, so the blue pigment turned up wearing the wrong shade. Fourteen years of work produced a rose that is chemically closer to blue than any rose in history and still looks lavender in the vase. Yellow was easier, and it cost more than anyone expected. Until about 1900, European garden roses came in white, pink, and red. A French breeder named Joseph Pernet-Ducher spent years crossing his roses with Rosa foetida, a tough yellow species from Asia, and finally produced a yellow garden rose he called Soleil d'Or. Essentially every yellow and orange rose sold today descends from that work. So does something else. Rosa foetida is badly susceptible to black spot, a fungus that strips a rose of its leaves, and the susceptibility rode into the modern rose holding hands with the color. Gardeners have been spraying for it ever since. One gene pool arrived carrying a gift and a bill. Scent has the strangest history of the three. In most flowering plants, the road to a scent molecule like geraniol runs through a family of enzymes called terpene synthases. When French researchers went looking for those enzymes in rose petals in 2015, the strongly scented roses were not using them at all. The roses were building geraniol by a completely different route, with an enzyme nobody had connected to scent before. The scentless varieties carried that same gene and were barely switching it on. The rose, it turns out, invented its own way to smell like a rose. Set those three stories side by side and a pattern surfaces. A rose is not a design. It is an accumulation: a pile of tools inherited from ancestors that were solving their own problems in their own centuries, some tools missing, some borrowed, some wired up in ways nobody predicted. We can move a gene from a pansy into a rose. We cannot ask a rose for a color it has never had, and we cannot take one trait without taking whatever else is holding hands with it. The rose in the vase looks simple. It is the least simple thing on the table.
